transcript.text: my belling cooker keeps burnin stuff 1 day then next day its undercookd on same temp. been like it a cuple months. thermastat??

Yes, it could be the thermostat — but it depends on the pattern. If the whole oven is sometimes far hotter than the setting and burns food even at a low setting, the temperature control is a strong suspect: a thermostat on a dial-controlled oven, or a temperature sensor/control fault on a digital oven. If it is mainly one side or the top burning while another area is undercooked, poor heat circulation, a door seal issue, or an oven element/function problem is more likely than the thermostat. Before assuming a fault, check:
1. Use the same oven function each time — not grill, rapid heat/booster, or a different conventional/fan setting. Fan-oven recipes normally need about 10–20°C less than conventional-oven recipes.
2. Avoid blocking airflow with several trays or placing food very close to an element. That can give burnt tops but underdone centres.
3. With the oven cold, check that the door closes flush and the seal is not split, loose or flattened. A leaking door can make results erratic. Is it a simple temperature dial, or does it have a digital temperature display—and when it burns food, is the whole dish overcooked or mainly one side/top?

its just knobs, no display, only a neon light. door shuts ok but the seal is a bit flattened at the top corner. mostly its the whole thing burnt or still cold in the middle, like my lasagne last week was cold in the middle after the usual time

A thermostat fault is now the leading possibility. On a knob-controlled oven, a thermostat that is drifting or sticking can let the whole oven run far too hot on one occasion, then fail to maintain enough heat on another. The flattened seal may lose a little heat, but it would not usually explain food being burnt one day and cold in the middle another. A weak/intermittent heating element or connection is the next possibility, particularly if the oven sometimes takes much longer than normal to heat. That more often causes undercooking than random overheating, so it is less likely than the thermostat. 1. Put an oven thermometer on the centre shelf, set the oven to 180°C on the function you normally use, and leave it for 25–30 minutes. Do not dismantle anything. - If it is well above about 200°C, or keeps climbing without settling, the thermostat is very likely not regulating. - If it is well below about 170°C or heats very slowly, an element, its connection, or the thermostat is not supplying/maintaining heat properly. 2. It should normally go out once near temperature, then come back on intermittently to maintain it. - Never going out supports an over-reading thermostat. - Going out early while the thermometer remains too cool points more towards the thermostat sensing incorrectly; erratic or very slow heating also keeps the element/circuit in consideration. If the thermometer suggests a large temperature swing, this is an engineer repair rather than a seal-only issue: thermostat replacement and checks of the heating circuit involve access to mains-wired parts. The seal is still worth replacing if it is badly flattened or split, but it is unlikely to be the main fault here.
i dont have a oven thermometer sorry. the neon goes off after 10 mins some days but other days it seems to stay on for ages. is that any help?

Yes, that is useful. The neon is the heat-demand light: it stays on while the control is asking the oven to heat, then should cycle on and off once temperature is reached. The fact that it goes out after about 10 minutes on some occasions but stays on for a long time on others supports a genuine heat-control fault rather than the slightly flattened seal. The leading cause remains the dial thermostat not regulating consistently. An intermittent heating element, connection or function-selector contact is also possible, especially if the light stays on but the oven is still not getting properly hot. For the next use, start with the oven cold, use the same cooking function and temperature setting as usual, and avoid opening the door repeatedly. Watch the neon and the heating behaviour:
1. Neon stays on and the oven becomes excessively hot or burns food: points to the thermostat/control failing to regulate.
2. Neon stays on but the oven is slow or weak and food remains undercooked: more suggestive of an element or its electrical connection/control path.
3. If it ever trips the electrics, stop using that oven and arrange an engineer; that can indicate an element insulation fault. Given the repeated burnt-or-undercooked results over months, I would avoid relying on it for food that needs a dependable cooking temperature, particularly poultry or reheated dishes. This needs an engineer to test the thermostat and heating circuit safely; it is not something to replace from the outside of the cooker.
